Paris, Friday. The Patrie, says þÿ þÿ The departure < f Lor i Cowley for Vienna lias been, yesterday and today, the subject of much commentary. Public opinion has given to this mission a great importance, and we believe that it is light. A letter from Vienna, of the 20th, in the Augsburg Gazette , says: þÿ þÿ The Austrian Government has obtained from the Holy See a promise that Cardinal Brunelli shall proceed to Paris to request the French Government to state, in clear and precise terms, the reforms which it wishes to see introduced in the States of the Church. THE PACIFICATION OF OUDE. Tlio following is an extract from a private letter, dated Lucknow, January 12 , - þÿ Since I last wrote to you the progress of events in Oudo has been roost rapid. The rebellion lias been quite quelled. There is not a man in arm hostilely opposed to þÿ is. The rebels trusted a good deal to their torts and forgot the power of our vertical fire. After one or two examples had been made, they found their forts were only traps, and that if they icniained in them they could not escape. Their jungles did not stop our troops, who no sooner appeared than they (the rebels) fled, and seeing opposition was useless, and that our amnesty was really meant to be one, which at first they would not believe, they came in and submitted ; and, sanguine as 1 ever have been, the result is beyond anything I had hoped for. The whole oountry is prostrate at our feat ; the forts are being demolished ;

three-fourths are already down ; the arms are Ih i i g given up, or forcibly taken; nearly 400, COO have been secured, and 1 shall require one and a half million before I am satisfied. The revenue is pouring in, and God has indeed greatly blessed and prospered all our doings. The army is breaking up. The Coiiiuiander-in-Chicf is on his way back to Lucknow, having lei t a good brigade on the Nepaul border The Begum, the Nana, and some others (but the rest of no note) are exceptions, and they are with the Begum, have taken advantage of the amnesty. A body of 15,000 military police will be distributed through the country, arid the Scinde police system is being introduced. All hopes of a pacific termination of the difficulties in Europe have been suddenly extinguished j by the invasion of Sardinian soil by the Austrians. Austria has, no doubt, precipitated matters by this course ; but, it cannot be denied, that she has acted with but ordinary prudence, in thus averting the blow which else was sure to fall. Austria has thus far outdone the French. With an army resolutely led, she might begin an entertainment quite contrary to the hopes of Louis Napoleon and M. Cavonr, before the French could interpose in force. The Austrians passed from their own territory to that of Sardinia in three columns. One of their divisions has penetrated the country from the North, landing on the Sardinian shores of the Lago Magf;iorc, anza, and Arona, and driving back the occupying the towns of Intra, Pal- Sardinians by the superiority of their numbers; a second, consisting of 20 battalions and eight batteries, has taken the road by Gravellona, and the third has found its way by Abbiati Grasso.

( From the London Times , April 30. ) Those who have studied the newspapers during the last two days must have suspected the vanity of telegrams and the baselessness of authentic information. Doubt has reigned as to facts which ought to be notorious, and contradictious have been given to statements made on the highest authority, and believed by the Government of the country. YVe endeavour to give the public all the information which interrupted posts and jealously watched telegraphs will allow ; but we must forewarn them that often during the course of the coming events they may be misled for 24 hours or longer by the unfounded rumours which prevail over the Coutinent. As yet, however, there has been no great inaccuracy in the information received. First, as regards the movements of the Austrians. From intelligence received yesterday we learn that the statement that an act of war was committed on the night of the 26th by the entry of Austrian troops on j Piedmontese soil was perfectly correct. The advanced posts of General Gyulai's army crossed the Ticino, and took up, unopposed, a position on the enemy's territory. But the advance of the main army did not take place till yesterday, April the 29th. By all accounts the Austrians had determined on a vigorous offensive movement, and there can be little doubt that they are desirous of striking a blow before French reinforcements can be brought into the field against them. So much for the proceedings at, the seat of war, on which we give as trustworthy

information as is to be had. With respect to the two Treaties or Conventions, or engagements, between France and Russia, we have nothing essential to retract In fact, we may leave our contemporaries to answer themselves, or each other. One of them has reason to kuow that the Russian Court has given þÿ that no agreement has been entered into that our Government the strongest assurances can in auy way affect the interests of this counþÿtry. As a commentary on this reassuring piece ot news, it states that a Russian army of 60,000 men has crossed the Dnieper, thereby threatening the Gallician frontier of Austria. Another journal, after giving the world to understand that we were utterly, wilfully, and scandalously wrong in stating that Russia had signed agreements with France, adds, with startling coolness, that the offensive and defensive alliance is only to take effect in case Germany or England should meddle in the quarrel. The moderation of France and Russia, in restricting themselves to a contingent, and not a direct, plot against a

friendly and mediating Power, receives, of course, its due tribute of admiration. In the midst of these vagaries and contradictions we have only to persist in the essential truth of our statement. It is not in the nature of a Secret Treaty to be known in its details within a week after signature, and consequently we do not pretend to give the entire purport of the document said to have been signed ou Good Friday. But the main facts are, we fear, beyond a doubt, and þÿ when we are informed that þÿ or Convention has been signed between Russia no secret Treaty þÿ and France, but that there exists an engageþÿ meut to place an army of observation on the þÿ Gallician þÿfrontier, we arc justified in believing that it is only that part of the engagement which cannot be denied that is confessed, aud that the execution of the other conditions waits only the development of events. While people here are affecting to doubt whether Napoleon and Alexander have been treacherous enough to deceive Lord Malmesbury, we find that at Berlin and Vienna uo doubt prevails as to the movement of Russian troops, threatening Posen and Gnllicia, and by the event we are willing that the truth of our statements should be judged. With regard to the actual state and the prospects of the campaign in Piedmont all must be speculation for þÿ clearly known, that the French were unpre- the present. One thing alone is pared for tho sudden move of the Austrians, and expected to begin the war at their leisure,

somewhere about the end of May. The difficulty and delay on Mont Cenis will be considerable, and, though the French arc being rapidly carried to Genoa, they are said to arrive there without tho means of entering on a campaign for a fortnight or three weeks It is difficult to learn the truth in these cases, and the French may have a direct object in inducing General Gyulai to believe in their difficulties; but a belief prevails that they will be unable to offer a serious resistance to the Austrians, should the latter determine on a vigorous and rapid attack.

THE NEW ATLANTIC TELEGRAPH. At last the long-pending question as to the probability of telegraphic communication being established between this country and America seems in a fair way of being settled. While the old Atlantic Telegraph Company has been wasting the money of the shareholders and seeking preposterous conditions from the Government, to guaranteee them from the evils of their own scientific mismanagement, a new company has been quietly formed under the best auspices, and, without troubling the Government about subsidies, or anything else, have carefully matured their plans with such foresight and deliberation as to lead the electrical world to look forward confidently to a successful solution of this great submarine enterprise. The British Transatlantic Telegraph Company propose, within this year if pos-ible, to lay their cable from the þÿLand s-cnd, in Cornwall, to Blanc Sabi on, an island in the Straits of Belle Isle, at one of the entrances of the Gulf of St. Lawrence, and a little to the north of Newfoundland A short wire, to be laid by a separate mpany, takes the cable in from Blanc Sablon to the Island of Anticosti where it meets lines already open, communicating with Quebec, Montreal, and, indeed, all parts of Canada. Another short line from Anticosti will he submerged to Cape Breton, where it will join the network of lines which communicate with Halifax, Nova Scotia, Bos'on, New York, &c. The advantages which such a toute presents over one starting from the west coa>t of Ireland are

immense, both in point of economy and freedom from the submarine dangers which beset the traek from Valentia to Newfoundland. In the fi -st place, the average depth of the entire route is supposed to be less, while by starting f rom þÿLand s-end the steep range of submarine mountains on the wcst-coast of Ireland, on which the Atlantic telegraph was so carelessly lost, is entirely avoided. On the Atlantic side, the liucs not being hampered with such preposterous conditions for messages as those which would check their transmission over Newfoundland, the tariff for their re-transmission will be less than one-half of what would bo charged if sent by the American Company from St. þÿJohn s, while the line, being all submerged, is, of course, less exposed to injury than in crossing the almost unexplored wilds of Newfoundland. Oa this side of the water tlio advantages of having the terminus at þÿLand s-end are almost greater. The increased distance is very little over 150 miles ; but a message arriving at þÿLand s-end is transmitted direct to its destination at a small cost, while the cost from Valentia is much greater, and the message itself lias to be re-transmitted always four times, and sometimes oftener. If it merely avoided the necessity of messages coming Irom America to Loudon being first known at Liverpool, where by the Irish route they must be transmitted, the gain to merchants by a þÿLand s-end teuninus would be most important. Morphy, the American Chess Player. On Tuesday evening, the 26th, the powers of this extraordinary player were put to a severe test in a match which came off at the St. þÿJames s Chess Club, þÿRegent s-quadrant, in which Mr. Morphy played simultaneously five of the most expert players of the club, including its president, Mr. Lowenthal. The tables were arranged in a row, each table beiug occupied on the odo side by a player, and on the other a passage W".3 left free, along which their single antagonist might pass backwards and forwards. Mr. Morphy is a man of small stature and rather juvenile appearance, but his head is exceedingly well formed, his eye bright, and bis countenance generally gives the evidence of a fine nervous organisation and quick intelligence. lie seems to play perfectly at his ease, generally making his moves with rapidity, although sometimes stopping and seeming to give the move in band a good deal of careful consideration. We endeavoured to ascertain whether, like other great players, lie had any favourite move or leading idea in his play, and there did seem to be a little uniformity in the eases in which he obtained the first move. But as this happened only in two eases out of the five, he was in the other three necessary influenced by the opening of his opponent. Speaking generally his style of play seems to he rapid and impetuous, and his þÿ coup d 'ceil þÿ so perfect that he can master at one glance all the exigencies of the board. More than once

in the course of the play his opponent had to call for time, which he conceded with the most good-humoured courtesy, chatting in the interim with whoever chanced to stand near him. The great secret of his success, over and above great practical skill as a chess player, would appear to lie in the wonderful powers and tenacity of his memory. We have seen men who could balance ten dinner plates, or ride six horses at once, but in those cases the act was at least imperfectly done. Mr. þÿMorphy case s is different. He plays the most abstruse and reflective ot known games, and plays it with a given number of the best known players, and the only advantage he has is the prestige of his wonderful name which certainly had considerable effect in producing caution on the part of all his opponents. The games took place in the elegant and capacious smokingroom of the St. þÿJames R s estaurant, and all the players to which Mr. Morphy was opposed worshipped the fuliginous genius of the place. þÿ observed, however, that he did not Smoke an We important fact tor the advocates of the counterblast. If any one required a particularly clear head it would be a man who, single-handed, undertook to play chess against five of the best players in London, and Mr. Morphy, although an American, would appear to deny himself his cigar in order to secure tho necessary amount of cerebral lucidity. The players against Mr Morphy were þÿ first table, M. do Riviere ; second, Mr. S. Boden ; third, Mr. W. Barnes; fourth, Mr. Bird; fifth,

Mr. Lowenthal. The play commenced at six þÿo clock, and was kept up with great spirit till a late hour of the night. The following was the result The game at the first table was won by Mr. Morphy ; at the second the game was drawn ; the third it was woti by Mr. Barnes ; at the fourth by Mr. Morphy ; at the fifth it was drawn.
